title: Control Plane High Traffic Audit

surfaces.risk: High request volume crosses the same handler middleware, route matching, authorization, and JSON response path.
surfaces.candidate: Keep route pattern metrics bounded, avoid per-request dynamic route labels, and benchmark response helpers before changing endpoint shapes.

surfaces.risk: Daemon poll, long-poll waiters, and assignment lease decisions can add channel and timer pressure under many idle agents.
surfaces.candidate: Keep long-poll waiters outside the actor critical path and track goroutine deltas in local pressure evidence.

surfaces.risk: Workspace SSE can accumulate subscribers and copy active thread filters while many clients watch the same task.
surfaces.candidate: Prefer active stream target projection and add leak checks before increasing SSE fanout.

surfaces.risk: Thread history v3 reconstructs historical user, progress, and agent messages, so refresh cost can grow with long conversations.
surfaces.candidate: Measure per-thread message copy cost, keep agent snapshots by id, and cap projection work before adding richer timelines.

surfaces.risk: Fine-grained provider output can create many normalize, merge, render, and fanout operations.
surfaces.candidate: Batch tiny provider fragments into line or frame sized updates while preserving v2/v3 response shapes.

surfaces.risk: Snapshot, split snapshot, assignment journal, active assignment, and stream relay paths drive RCU/WCU and transaction contention.
surfaces.candidate: Attribute costs by operation vocabulary and keep snapshot read models split from write-command models.

surfaces.risk: HTTP and store metric windows are intentionally bounded but still run on every hot path.
surfaces.candidate: Keep lock scope copy-only, preserve top-N output, and watch allocation per operation in benchmarks.

assertions: This audit must not change endpoint paths, request bodies, response fields, or status semantics.
Every high-traffic surface must bind source files, static patterns, and a next optimization candidate.
Open-loop pressure evidence must record throughput, latency, allocation, heap, CPU, and goroutine deltas.
Open-loop pressure evidence must rank measured allocation, latency, CPU, and goroutine findings.
pprof evidence must remain loopback-only and must cover CPU, heap, and goroutine views.
Repeated bottlenecks found by this audit should be promoted into closed-loop candidates, not fixed from intuition alone.

loop.observation: Control-plane performance work already emits benchmarks and local pressure, but the risky source surfaces are not compiled into one auditable map.
loop.hypothesis: A static high-traffic audit can connect endpoint, store, SSE, scheduling, progress, DynamoDB, and metric hot paths to executable evidence before any API-neutral optimization.
loop.execute: Scan declared surfaces for high-risk primitives, verify pprof and stress commands, publish redacted audit evidence, and keep generated docs in sync.
loop.evaluate: The verifier fails on missing files, missing patterns, missing candidates, unsafe pprof commands, missing workflow artifact upload, or generated doc drift.
loop.retrospective: This keeps the first slice open-loop: observe pressure and source risk, then decide which bottlenecks deserve closed-loop gates.
